report:
**Conclusion: No.** High-quality randomized evidence does not show that hydroxychloroquine reduces deaths from COVID-19.

The clearest direct evidence is the large UK RECOVERY randomized controlled trial in hospitalized patients. It found no improvement in 28-day mortality with hydroxychloroquine (and no benefit on hospital discharge or progression to mechanical ventilation/death). Random allocation is important because it avoids the confounding that can make early observational reports appear favorable.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2022926

Results also hold when trials are pooled. A meta-analysis of randomized trials assessing mortality found hydroxychloroquine was not associated with lower mortality; its results were driven by the large, well-conducted trials rather than small or uncontrolled studies.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33859192/

WHO’s current review is especially useful as a synthesis of the overall evidence: it reports findings from 30 trials involving more than 10,000 COVID-19 patients. Hydroxychloroquine did **not** reduce mortality, need for mechanical ventilation, or its duration, and WHO does not recommend it as COVID-19 treatment.  
https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/coronavirus-disease-(covid-19)-hydroxychloroquine

There are also safety reasons not to use it outside an appropriate clinical setting: hydroxychloroquine can cause potentially serious heart-rhythm effects and drug interactions. The FDA revoked its COVID-19 emergency authorization after concluding that the totality of evidence showed lack of benefit.  
https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/coronavirus-covid-19-update-fda-revokes-emergency-use-authorization-chloroquine-and

This concerns hydroxychloroquine for COVID-19; it remains an established prescription medicine for certain autoimmune diseases.
